exercises.prompt: What does a principle name, as against a prepared list of moves?

choices.text: The particular sentences to recite, fixed before any facts are known.
The kind of fact, and the kind of action that follows from that kind.
A gesture that counts as compliance even when the case was never judged.
The feeling that should accompany whatever action you already preferred.

feedback.note: A principle names the kind of fact and the kind of action that follows. It does not list the particular moves. A script pretends those moves are already written. A required feeling would be subjectivism, and a fixed recitation would replace judgment with a performance. The principle becomes usable when someone identifies the facts of the case.

exercises.prompt: What does a script pretend, where a principle does not?

choices.text: That the particular moves are already listed, before this case has been judged.
That the actor must identify what kind of fact this situation is.
That one principle can require a new action when the facts change.
That later principles rest on earlier ones in a fixed order.

feedback.note: A script pretends the particular moves are already listed, so the case never has to be judged. Identifying the kind of fact, and changing the action when the facts change, belong to the use of a principle. The error in a script is that it counterfeits a decision by writing the ending in advance, because the particulars were never judged.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the job it actually does.

pairs.left: A principle
pairs.right: Names the kind of fact and the kind of action that follows

pairs.left: A script
pairs.right: Pretends the particular moves are already listed

pairs.left: A concrete action
pairs.right: The particular move the facts of this case require

pairs.left: A slogan used in place of either
pairs.right: Stands in for both the fact and the action

feedback.note: A principle states a kind, and the concrete action is the particular that kind calls for once the facts are judged. A script skips that judgment by pretending the moves are prelisted. A slogan does neither job, because it replaces both the kind of fact and the action with a phrase. Keeping them apart is what stops a standard from being used as a prompt card.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast between a principle and a prewritten sequence.

parts.text: A principle names a kind of fact and action. A
pretends the particular moves are already listed.

feedback.note: A script is what pretends the particular moves are already listed. A fact does not pretend; it is what the judgment has to meet. An axiom and a virtue are not lists of moves either. The error is to call the script a principle, which confuses a standard that names a kind with a counterfeit that decides the particulars in advance.

exercises.prompt: Before any dispute exists, a person memorizes five replies in order. In the real dispute he speaks them and never identifies the claim being made. What did he use?

choices.text: A principle of justice, because the replies were delivered in order.
A script, because the moves were listed before the facts were judged.
Epistemology, because memorizing is itself a way of knowing the case.
A compromise, because five replies are enough to cover every side.

feedback.note: The replies were listed in advance, and he did not identify the claim in front of him, so the performance was a script. Orderly speech is not justice, because justice names the kind of fact, here what was actually claimed and done, and the kind of action that follows. Memorizing does not identify this case, and covering every side does not make a compromise.

exercises.prompt: Which request asks for a script rather than for a principle?

choices.text: Name the kind of fact that would show this contract is honest, and the action that follows.
Give the exact sentences, so I do not have to judge this contract.
State the virtue. I will read the terms before I sign.
If the terms change, say whether the same virtue still applies.

feedback.note: Asking for the exact sentences, so that judgment can be skipped, asks for a script, because a script pretends the moves are already listed. The other requests keep the principle in its proper job: naming the kind of fact and the kind of action, including when the terms change. The wish to be spared the judgment is what turns a standard into a counterfeit decision.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that says what a principle names.

feedback.note: A principle names the kind of fact and the kind of action, which is why it can guide many cases without listing them. A memorized speech is a script, and a feeling is a subjectivist substitute. Either one changes the claim, because neither names a kind of fact from which an action follows. The particular judgment stays with the person who has the facts.

exercises.prompt: A friend says a principle is useless unless it names the exact words to say in every case. What is she demanding?

choices.text: That a principle do the work of a script.
That a principle name the kind of fact and the kind of action.
That you identify the facts of the case before you speak.
That later principles keep their dependence on earlier ones.

feedback.note: Exact words for every case would be a script, which pretends the particulars are already listed. A principle is useful because it names the kind of fact and the kind of action, and the speaker judges this case. Her demand treats that open work as a defect. It is the feature that lets one standard cover cases no list could write out in advance.

exercises.prompt: What does applying a principle require in the situation you actually face?

choices.text: Judging the facts of this case under the kind the principle names.
Repeating the principle until the case feels settled.
Repeating the action you used last time, since the principle is unchanged.
Choosing whichever action would be most widely admired.

feedback.note: Application means judging the facts of this case, because a principle names a kind and the case shows whether this situation is of that kind. Repetition does not identify a fact. Last time's action ignores what may differ now, and admiration is subjectivism, a poll of feelings standing in for the facts. The principle does not do the looking for you.

exercises.prompt: Honesty here means refusing to fake reality. A contract is in front of you. Which action applies the principle to this case?

choices.text: Sign at once, because the word honesty has a good reputation.
Recite a definition of honesty and leave the pages unread.
Read the terms, identify what they claim, and refuse a signature that would fake that record.
Treat the other party's feeling as the content of the terms.

feedback.note: The facts of this case are the terms and what they claim. Honesty requires you to identify that record and not fake it, so reading, and refusing a signature that would fake it, is the application. Reputation and recitation leave the document out. Treating a feeling as the content of the terms is subjectivism, because a feeling is not the fact the principle told you to identify.

exercises.prompt: Match each move to its role in applying a principle.

pairs.left: Name the kind of fact and the kind of action
pairs.right: State the principle

pairs.left: Identify what is true in this situation
pairs.right: Judge the facts of this case

pairs.left: Let a slogan stand in for those facts
pairs.right: Skip the application

pairs.left: Do what that kind of fact requires here
pairs.right: Complete the application

feedback.note: Application has a shape. The principle names the kind, the person identifies the facts of this case, and the action is the one that kind requires here. A slogan that replaces the facts skips the middle step, so no application has occurred, because the slogan can be true and still go unused.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule that ties a principle to a situation.

parts.text: Applying a principle means judging the facts of

feedback.note: The facts that matter are the facts of this case, because the principle is general and the choice is particular. A slogan, last year's episode, or a crowd does not identify what is true here. Those substitutes are how a principle gets recited instead of applied. The judgment has to meet the situation in front of you.

exercises.prompt: A colleague says the facts of the dispute are optional, because the principle already contains the decision. What is the error?

choices.text: He is applying the principle by refusing to be distracted by detail.
He is letting the principle, shrunk to a slogan, stand in for the facts of this case.
He is tracing a contradicted conclusion back to an axiom.
He is changing the action because the facts of the case changed.

feedback.note: A principle does not contain the particular decision. It names a kind, and the decision comes from judging this case. Treating the facts as optional turns the principle into a slogan that stands in for them. That is not a response to changed facts, because the facts were never identified, and he is not examining an axiom. He is skipping the case.

exercises.prompt: Both parties feel sure. An observer says their feelings are the facts to which the principle applies. What error is that?

choices.text: Subjectivism: feelings are treated as if they were the facts of the case.
Correct application: sincerity is the kind of fact every principle names.
Identity: each feeling is what it is, so the feeling settles the dispute.
A package deal: the presence of two parties fuses their claims into one.

feedback.note: Subjectivism treats feelings as the facts, or as the values that settle the case. A feeling is a feeling, which is all that identity claims here, but it is not the fact a principle such as honesty or justice told you to judge. Sincerity is not the kind of fact those principles name. Two parties do not make a package deal. The observer still has to identify what was done.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule that keeps application tied to the situation in front of you.

feedback.note: Application judges the facts of this case. Reciting replaces that judgment with sound, and the crowd's mood replaces the facts with other people's feelings, which is subjectivism. Either substitute leaves the principle unused, because neither one identifies the facts of this case. The rule is what lets a general standard reach one particular choice.

exercises.prompt: Two employees each refuse a request. One refuses to sign a false report. One refuses to look at the figures. Honesty is the principle. What must you do before you praise or blame?

choices.text: Praise both, because both acts are called a refusal.
Blame both, because a refusal is always an evasion.
Judge the facts of each case. The shared word does not say who faked reality.
Skip judgment, because similar gestures fall under one script.

feedback.note: The word refusal covers two different facts. One person refused to fake a record; the other refused to identify it. Honesty names the kind of fact, a record that fakes reality or does not, so you have to judge which fact this case contains. Praising or blaming from the shared word lets a label stand in for the facts. A script would treat the gesture as enough.

exercises.prompt: The facts of a case change. What can change with them, and what stays?

choices.text: The principle changes, and the old action stays as a sign of loyalty.
Both must stay. A real standard never requires a different action.
The principle stays, and the concrete action can change.
Both must change. A new situation needs a new philosophy.

feedback.note: The principle names a kind of fact and a kind of action, so it stays while the particulars are judged again. When the facts change, the same principle can require a different concrete action. Keeping the old gesture out of loyalty treats the earlier action as if it were the principle. Replacing the philosophy treats a new particular as if it had erased the standard.

exercises.prompt: Justice requires paying for work that was done. Last month the work was done and you paid. This month the work was not done. What does the same principle require now?

choices.text: Pay again, because a principled action must not change.
Do not pay for work that was not done. The principle is unchanged.
Drop justice, because a principle that allows two actions contradicts itself.
Pay, because the worker feels that the payment is owed.

feedback.note: The kind of fact justice names is what the person did. Last month that fact required payment; this month it does not, so the concrete action changes and the principle stays. Calling that a contradiction confuses a new application with a new principle. Paying from the worker's feeling is subjectivism. Repeating the old payment lets a past action stand in for the present fact.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to what happens when the facts of a case change.

pairs.left: The principle
pairs.right: Stays, as the same standard

pairs.left: The concrete action
pairs.right: Can change under that standard

pairs.left: The new facts
pairs.right: Have to be judged before the action is chosen

pairs.left: Last time's gesture, copied automatically
pairs.right: Not an application to the new facts

feedback.note: A change of facts does not retire the principle. It requires a fresh judgment, and that judgment can require a different concrete action. Copying the last gesture skips the new facts, so it is not the principle remaining constant. It is a script made out of one earlier application.

exercises.prompt: Complete the point about one principle under new facts.

parts.text: The same principle can require a different

feedback.note: What can change is the concrete action, because the action is the particular and the principle is the standard. A new moral code, a new axiom, or a revelation would throw out the philosophy rather than apply it. The error in those substitutes is to treat a difference in the case as if it were a difference in the kind of fact the principle names.

exercises.prompt: A friend says that if your action changed, you abandoned the principle. What is the right answer?

choices.text: A changed action under the same standard is abandonment.
The first action remains binding, because a principle is a script.
A changed action can be the same principle applied to new facts.
A principle should be replaced whenever a new action is more convenient.

feedback.note: The friend mistakes a new concrete action for a new principle. The principle stays and names the kind; the facts decide the particular. Binding the first action forever is the script error. Replacing the principle when it is inconvenient is pragmatism, which treats the truth as whatever works at the moment. Neither one keeps the standard and judges the new facts.

exercises.prompt: Which policy keeps an old action in place after the facts that justified it are gone?

choices.text: Judge the new facts and do what the same principle now requires.
Treat the earlier action as if it were the principle itself.
Trace a contradicted conclusion back to the premise that produced it.
Name the earlier principles on which the policy rests.

feedback.note: Treating the earlier action as the principle freezes a particular and calls the freeze loyalty. The facts that made that action right are gone, so the same principle can require something else. Re-judging the new facts is the application. Tracing a premise does not lock the old gesture in place, because that trace answers a different problem.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that keeps the standard while allowing a new action.

feedback.note: The same principle can require a different concrete action when the facts change, because the principle names a kind and the case supplies the particular. Abandoning the principle throws out the standard. Forbidding any change turns one application into a script. Both errors confuse the principle with a single gesture.

exercises.prompt: The facts change, the action changes, and the person adds that the principle is now optional because the old rule is no longer convenient. What has he done?

choices.text: He has applied one principle to new facts and kept the principle.
He has changed the action and also dropped the standard, which the new facts do not license.
He has shown that every principle is a script and ought to be dropped.
He has followed determinism: the facts changed him without a judgment.

feedback.note: New facts can require a different concrete action under the same principle. They do not make the principle optional. Dropping it because it is inconvenient is pragmatism: the truth is replaced by what works now. He did judge, so this is not determinism, and the principle was not shown to be a script. The error smuggles a rejection of the standard into a legitimate change of action.

exercises.prompt: You hold a principle and you know the facts of the case. Who judges it?

choices.text: The philosophy, acting as a substitute that decides in your place.
You, using the philosophy as a standard for your own thinking.
A crowd, because a standard is whatever most people would feel.
No one, because a real principle leaves nothing to judge.

feedback.note: The philosophy is a standard for your thinking. You have to identify the facts and judge. It is not a mind that decides the case for you. A crowd substitutes other people's feelings, which is subjectivism. The claim that nothing remains to judge confuses a standard with a script that has already listed the move. Holding the principle makes the judgment possible. It does not perform the judgment.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks what the philosophy would choose for a meal, a sentence, and a verdict. What is wrong with the question?

choices.text: Nothing. A philosophy that cannot pick a meal is incomplete.
It treats the philosophy as a substitute decider rather than as a standard you use.
The question fails because meals fall outside the law of identity.
The question is right about the verdict and wrong only about the meal.

feedback.note: A standard does not choose a meal, a sentence, or a verdict. You choose, by judging the facts under the principles. The question turns the philosophy into a substitute mind. Meals do not fall outside identity, and the error is the same for the verdict as for the meal: the principle names the kind of fact, and the person has to judge the particular. Completeness is not the power to skip that act.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the role it can actually fill.

pairs.left: The philosophy
pairs.right: A standard for your own thinking

pairs.left: You
pairs.right: The one who judges this case

pairs.left: A slogan asked to deliver the verdict
pairs.right: A substitute pretending to decide

pairs.left: A revelation said to settle the case
pairs.right: Mysticism in place of your judgment

feedback.note: The philosophy supplies the standard, and you judge the case by it. A slogan asked to deliver the verdict pretends to be a substitute mind. A revelation does the same work by mysticism, because it claims a source beyond reason that settles the case without your judgment. Neither one is a standard you are using. Both leave the case unjudged.

exercises.prompt: Complete the account of what a philosophy is for when a case has to be decided.

parts.text: A philosophy is a standard for your own
, not a substitute that decides the case.

feedback.note: The philosophy is a standard for your own thinking, which means you identify and judge. Feelings, orders, or habits do not judge the case; they replace the act. A substitute that decides in your place would leave you with nothing to do, and that is the error. The standard makes thinking responsible. It does not retire thinking.

exercises.prompt: Which request hands the case to a substitute so that you do not have to judge it?

choices.text: Name the principle. I will identify the facts and decide.
Here are the facts. Name the kind of action, and I will look again if I misread them.
Do not explain the standard. Deliver the verdict, so the philosophy has decided.
If I have misidentified the facts, the conclusion has to be checked.

feedback.note: Asking for a bare verdict, so that the philosophy has decided, treats the philosophy as a substitute. The other requests keep the judgment with the person: name the standard, identify the facts, and check a conclusion if the facts were misread. Those are uses of a standard. The third request wants the result of thinking without the thinking.

exercises.prompt: A listener says you cannot judge the case, because the outcome was already fixed and principles are commentary after the fact. Which error is that?

choices.text: Determinism: it denies the judgment a standard exists to guide.
A correct account of a standard, because standards describe and never guide.
The trader principle, because every case is an exchange of feelings.
Esthetics, because every choice is a staged performance.

feedback.note: Determinism denies that you judge, so it makes a standard pointless: there is no choice for the principle to guide. A standard is for thinking that directs action, not commentary attached afterward. Trade and esthetics are real principles in their own places, and neither says the outcome was fixed before you judged. The error leaves the facts and the principle with no one to connect them.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that keeps the judgment in the person's hands.

feedback.note: The philosophy is a standard you use to judge, so the thinking remains yours. Calling it a substitute hands the case to a counterfeit decider. Calling it a ritual turns the use into a ceremony of gestures. Either change removes the act the standard exists to guide, because you still have to identify the facts and reach the conclusion.

exercises.prompt: You misread the figures, apply justice to that misreading, and reach a wrong verdict. You then say the philosophy decided, so the verdict cannot be an error. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing. A standard guarantees the particular conclusion.
The excuse treats the philosophy as a substitute. The misreading is still your error.
Justice cannot be applied to a record of figures.
A wrong verdict shows that no principle can guide a case.

feedback.note: The standard did not decide, and it does not guarantee a verdict reached from a misidentified fact. You judged, and you judged on a bad reading, so the error is yours. Crediting the philosophy treats it as a substitute. The skeptical conclusion, that no principle can guide, is wider than the evidence. Check the facts, then apply the principle again. Justice applies to what was done, including a record in figures.

exercises.prompt: What distinguishes holding a principle in ordinary life from turning practice into a ritual?

choices.text: A ritual judges ordinary choices, while a principle only decorates them.
A principle is used to judge ordinary choices. A ritual performs gestures and leaves the choice unjudged.
A principle is valid only inside a ceremony, so the ritual is the real standard.
There is no distinction, because every repeated action is a ritual.

feedback.note: Holding a principle means judging ordinary choices by the kind of fact and the kind of action it names. A ritual performs gestures and leaves the choice unjudged. Repetition alone is not the error, because a standing policy can be principled. The error is the ceremony that substitutes motions for judgment. A principle is not reserved for staged occasions.

exercises.prompt: Each morning a man recites the names of the virtues, then signs a report he has not read. What did the recitation accomplish?

choices.text: It applied the virtues to the report.
It was a ritual of gestures, and the report was left unjudged.
It made the signature honest, because a preface validates a document.
It changed the facts of the report by being sincere.

feedback.note: Naming the virtues on a schedule did not identify what the report claimed. The unread signature is the choice, and honesty was not applied to it. Sincerity does not change the facts, and a preface does not make an unread record honest. The recitation was a ritual: the gestures were performed and the concrete choice was left untouched.

exercises.prompt: Match each practice to what it comes to.

pairs.left: Checking a figure before you sign
pairs.right: Applying a principle to an ordinary choice

pairs.left: Reciting virtue-names and not looking
pairs.right: A ritual of gestures

pairs.left: A fixed speech, whatever the page says
pairs.right: A script

pairs.left: Judging the page when nobody is watching
pairs.right: A principle held in ordinary life

feedback.note: An ordinary choice is still a choice, so the principle applies when you check the figure and when nobody is watching. Recitation without looking is a ritual, because the gesture replaced the judgment. A fixed speech that ignores the page is a script, because the moves were treated as already listed. Ceremony and prelisting are different ways of not judging the case.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast between practice and ceremony.

parts.text: Hold the principles in ordinary choices, not in a ritual of

feedback.note: The rejected item is a ritual of gestures, motions that stand in for thinking. Facts, standards, and judgments are what ordinary practice uses, so they do not name the error. A ceremony can be sincere and still leave the choice unjudged, because the gesture is not an identification of the facts. The principles belong in the choices.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is an ordinary application, rather than a ceremony?

choices.text: Wearing an emblem so that observers will classify you as principled.
Comparing a wage to the work actually done before you agree to it.
Reciting a motto at the table and leaving a contract unread.
Keeping a list of postures to assume whenever a principle is named.

feedback.note: Comparing the wage to the work is justice applied to an ordinary agreement: you judge this fact and then act. An emblem, a motto, and a list of postures are gestures. They can be performed while the agreement goes unexamined, so they are ritual. None of them names the kind of fact the principle requires you to identify. The ordinary case is where the standard has its use.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says that if the gestures were performed correctly, the choice was moral, whether or not anyone identified the facts. Which error is that?

choices.text: Intrinsicism about the gesture: the performance is treated as carrying the value by itself.
Application: a correct form is the kind of fact a principle names.
Primacy of existence: a gesture is physical, so the performance is the judgment.
Hierarchy: gestures come first, and the facts are derived from them.

feedback.note: Intrinsicism treats the value as residing in the object, here the performed gesture, with no method and no need to judge the facts. A principle names a kind of fact, not a choreography. That the gesture is physical does not make the performance a moral judgment, and hierarchy does not put motions ahead of facts. The choice is moral or not by the action under the standard.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that puts principles into ordinary choices.

feedback.note: The principles are held across ordinary choices, without a ritual of gestures. A public ceremony and a checklist of poses can both be completed while the choice itself is never judged, so they are the substitutes the line rejects. The sentence does not condemn a repeated true policy. It condemns the performance that stands in for thinking.

exercises.prompt: Nobody will notice an error left in a report. You say no principle applies, because the occasion is too small for a moral ceremony. What is the mistake?

choices.text: None. Principles apply only on occasions large enough for a ceremony.
You are confining the philosophy to ritual occasions and leaving an ordinary choice unjudged.
Honesty forbids correcting an error, because correction admits a fault.
A small error is metaphysically given and cannot be changed.

feedback.note: Honesty names a kind of fact, a record that fakes reality or does not, and this report is that kind of fact. The size of the audience does not retire the principle. Confining it to ceremonial occasions turns practice into a ritual and leaves ordinary life unprincipled. The error is man-made, so it can be corrected. Correction is the action the principle requires here, and you are the one who has to judge that.

exercises.prompt: What makes a set of ideas one philosophic system, rather than several opinions kept side by side?

choices.text: They form one integrated view of existence.
Each line is kept because it sounds bold on its own.
They match whatever the holder prefers that day.
Each line counts as true because it once paid off.

feedback.note: A philosophic system is one integrated view of existence, so the claims have to belong to a single account of what is. A pile of favorite lines fails because each one is saved for its sound and none has to agree with the others. Preference is subjectivism, and a payoff is pragmatism: neither one integrates claims into a view of existence.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the nature of a philosophic system?
exercises.quote: A philosophic system is an integrated view of existence.

choices.text: It is a catalog that gathers the special sciences.
It is one integrated view of existence.
It is a mood that changes whenever feelings change.
It is a political program with no claim about what exists.

feedback.quote: A philosophic system is an integrated view of existence.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Philosophy: Who Needs It," Philosophy: Who Needs It, 5
feedback.note: The passage states the requirement directly: a philosophic system is an integrated view of existence. A catalog of the sciences fails because a list of fields is not one account of what exists. A mood fails because feelings are not that account, and a political program with no claim about existence has left the integration out.

exercises.prompt: Match each collection of ideas to the kind of outlook it is.

pairs.left: Claims that fit as one account of what exists
pairs.right: An integrated philosophic system

pairs.left: Favorite lines kept without having to agree
pairs.right: A pile of slogans

pairs.left: One admired sentence, left unconnected
pairs.right: A detached slogan

pairs.left: Lines accepted because they match today's feelings
pairs.right: A subjectivist collection

feedback.note: An integrated system is marked by claims that fit one view of existence. A pile, a detached slogan, and a subjectivist collection fail that test, because none of them requires the claims to agree about what is. Liking a line, or feeling it, does not perform the integration.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast between a system and a stack of sayings.

parts.text: A philosophy is an
view, not a
of slogans.

feedback.note: Integrated names the demand that the claims form one view of existence. A pile does not meet it, because the parts are only collected. Private or shifting would turn the view into a preference, which is subjectivism, and would leave the system unstated. The two words belong in that order because only that order names one outlook.

exercises.prompt: A reader keeps three lines he likes: trust your feelings, follow the evidence, and obey the majority. He never asks whether they can share one outlook. What does he hold?

choices.text: One system, because any three sincere lines are a philosophy.
A pile of slogans, because the lines were never required to fit.
An integrated view, because conflict among lines shows depth.
A hierarchy, because a list is already an order of dependence.

feedback.note: These lines do not form one view of existence, because a feeling, the evidence, and a majority cannot jointly settle what is. The error is treating admired sentences as a system while they contradict one another. A real integration would drop the claims that cannot belong together, rather than saving each one for its appeal.

exercises.prompt: A speaker calls her mix of lines a philosophy because she finds the mix inspiring and she chose it. Which error is that?

choices.text: Subjectivism: preference is treated as if it welded the claims into one view.
Skepticism: she is denying that any claim about existence can be formed.
Determinism: the mix is said to have assembled itself without a choice.
Mysticism: an unspoken revelation is offered as the integrating act.

feedback.note: Subjectivism is the error, because the fact that she prefers the lines is treated as if preference made them one view of existence. Inspiration does not make claims agree. Skepticism does not fit, because she is offering a mixture rather than denying knowledge. Mysticism does not fit either, because she points to her choice, and choice alone does not integrate a system.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that keeps a philosophy distinct from a collection of sayings.

feedback.note: The statement names one integrated view of existence, which is what makes the claims a system. A pile of slogans or a wave of inspiration changes the claim, because those are the collections a system is being distinguished from. A feeling does not supply the missing agreement among the parts.

exercises.prompt: Someone accepts a view of existence, adds a moral rule that contradicts it, and calls the result one system because both parts are sincere. What is the mistake?

choices.text: Sincerity integrates claims even when they contradict one another.
Moral rules are decorations and never belong in a view of existence.
A contradiction means the parts are not one view, so the added rule broke it.
A system may ignore identity, since existence is prior to consistency.

feedback.note: One view of existence cannot house a contradiction, because contradictory claims are not a single account of what is. Sincerity does not integrate them; it only reports that the holder means both. A moral rule belongs in the system when it follows from that view. Dropping consistency would abandon identity, which dissolves the view rather than saving it.

exercises.prompt: In what order do the branches stand, so that each later principle has something earlier to rest on?

choices.text: Politics, then ethics, then epistemology, then metaphysics.
Metaphysics, then epistemology, then ethics, then politics.
Ethics first, because values decide which facts exist.
Epistemology first, because a method decides what is allowed to exist.

feedback.note: The order is metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and politics, because each later principle rests on the earlier account of what exists and of how one knows it. Starting from politics, or from values, reverses that dependence. Putting method before existence does the same thing in epistemological dress: consciousness is treated as setting the facts it would have to know.

exercises.prompt: Match each branch to the question it answers inside the system.

pairs.left: Metaphysics
pairs.right: What exists

pairs.left: Epistemology
pairs.right: How one knows

pairs.left: Ethics
pairs.right: What to value

pairs.left: Politics
pairs.right: The social principle

feedback.note: Metaphysics states what exists, and the later branches rest on that, because each one presupposes the question before it. Epistemology then asks how one knows, ethics asks what to value, and politics states the social principle. Swapping the questions would let a later branch pretend to stand without the earlier one it needs. The names are an order of dependence, rather than interchangeable labels.

exercises.prompt: Why is that order part of the philosophy, rather than a convenient sequence for a syllabus?

choices.text: Later principles rest on earlier ones, so a reversal leaves them without a base.
The labels are traditional, and any order would carry the same claims.
Politics is first in practice, and the other branches are commentary.
Each branch is self-contained, so the sequence is a matter of taste.

feedback.note: The order is logical, because a claim about value or about society presupposes what exists and how one knows it. Calling the sequence a syllabus convenience, or a matter of taste, treats the branches as self-contained modules. They are not. A later principle with the earlier ones removed has nothing left that it can rest on.

exercises.prompt: Complete the dependence that makes the order necessary.

parts.text: Later principles rest on

feedback.note: Later principles rest on earlier ones, because a value or a social rule cannot be known apart from what exists and how one knows. A majority, a feeling, or a revelation does not supply that base. Those substitutes skip the branches the later principle depends on, and they leave the principle with nothing that could show it is true.

exercises.prompt: Where does esthetics stand relative to one's view of man and of existence?

choices.text: It is an optional extra, attached once the social principle is finished.
It replaces metaphysics, because an image decides what exists.
It depends on the view of man and of existence.
It is the social principle, stated in another vocabulary.

feedback.note: Esthetics depends on the view of man and of existence, because a work selects reality according to a fundamental appraisal of both. Treating it as an optional extra leaves that dependence out. Treating an image as if it decided what exists reverses the order, and renaming politics as esthetics confuses a social principle with an appraisal of man and of existence.

exercises.prompt: A campaigner defends a social system, then says that questions about what exists or how she knows it are irrelevant to politics. What has she denied?

choices.text: Nothing important, because politics is the first branch.
That a social principle rests on metaphysics and epistemology.
That politics is a branch of the philosophy at all.
That people are permitted to argue about policy.

feedback.note: Politics is the social principle, and it rests on what exists and on how one knows, because those earlier branches are its base. Calling them irrelevant takes the later branch off that base. She has not denied that politics is a branch. She has denied the dependence that gives it standing. Argument about policy does not replace that base.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that states how later principles stand.

feedback.note: Later principles rest on earlier ones, so metaphysics and epistemology are not optional prefaces to ethics and politics. A vote replaces that dependence with numbers, and the claim that later principles float free treats them as self-supporting. A social principle with nothing earlier under it has nothing left that could validate it.

exercises.prompt: A theorist says the mind's forms structure experience, so we must settle how the mind shapes objects before we may say what exists. What has he done to the order?

choices.text: He has kept it, because epistemology is only a short preface.
He has kept it, because consciousness properly sets the identity of what exists.
He has reversed it, by putting the mind's structure ahead of what exists.
He has left philosophy, because order among branches is a private preference.

feedback.note: This reverses the chain, because the account of what exists comes before the account of how one knows. The theorist's claim is the Kantian one: the mind's forms structure experience, so we do not reach things as they are, and method swallows existence. Preference does not make the order optional. Later principles cannot rest on a base that consciousness is said to invent.

exercises.prompt: What is meant by an idea pulled out of the middle of the philosophy?

choices.text: An axiom, stated before any other principle.
An idea cut away from the earlier principles that support it.
A concrete choice that nobody has faced yet.
A branch taught last, and therefore the deepest one.

feedback.note: A middle idea depends on earlier principles. Pulling it out means keeping the idea and dropping the premises that support it. An axiom is not in the middle, because no prior principle is required to state it. A concrete choice is an application, and being taught last does not by itself cut a branch off from its base.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the place it occupies.

pairs.left: The account of what exists, kept as the base
pairs.right: An earlier principle, not a middle idea

pairs.left: An ethical principle quoted with no view of existence
pairs.right: An idea pulled out of the middle

pairs.left: A social principle still tied to the ethics it needs
pairs.right: An idea still inside the chain

pairs.left: A wish about policy, never derived from a principle
pairs.right: Not a middle idea, because it was never in the chain

feedback.note: A middle idea is a later principle, and it stays in the chain only while it rests on earlier ones. Quoting an ethical principle with no view of existence pulls it out. A wish is a different failure, because a wish was never a principle in the chain. Metaphysics is earlier, so it is not itself something that can be pulled from the middle.

exercises.prompt: An advocate repeats that a person is an end in himself, then refuses every question about what a person is or how anyone knows it. What has he done?

choices.text: He has validated the claim by refusing to dilute it.
He has pulled the claim out of the middle, away from the premises that support it.
He has returned the claim to metaphysics, where it belongs as an axiom.
He has applied the claim, because repetition is a form of use.

feedback.note: The claim that a person is an end in himself is an ethical principle, so it rests on what a person is and on how one knows that. Refusing those questions cuts the idea off from its premises. Repetition does not validate it or apply it, and the claim is not an axiom of metaphysics. It is a middle idea being treated as if it stood alone.

exercises.prompt: Complete the description of an idea pulled out of the middle.

parts.text: It is cut away from the
that support it.

feedback.note: The support for a middle idea is the earlier principles it rests on. A feeling, a revelation, or a vote cannot take their place, because none of those is the base the idea was derived from. Cutting the earlier principles away is what it means to pull the idea out of the middle. A later wish is not a substitute base.

exercises.prompt: Which item is not an idea pulled out of the middle?

choices.text: A right, asserted with no account of what a person is.
The principle that existence exists, offered as a start rather than as a deduction.
A virtue, praised in a speech that never connects it to human life.
A social system, defended while every question about rights is waved away.

feedback.note: Existence exists is an axiomatic start, not a middle idea, because it does not rest on a prior principle one could cut away. A right, a virtue, or a social system can be pulled out, because each rests on earlier claims. Waving those claims away is the detachment. It does not promote a derivative principle into an axiom.

exercises.prompt: A reader says a political slogan needs no earlier premises, because its truth is simply present in the words. Which error is that?

choices.text: Intrinsicism: the slogan is treated as carrying its truth, with no method and no base.
The right order: a political claim is true before anything exists.
A proper validation: slogans of this kind are axioms.
Esthetics: any striking sentence is thereby known to be true.

feedback.note: Intrinsicism treats a content as revealed in the object, here the slogan, with no method and no need for earlier knowledge. A political principle is not an axiom, and it does not come before existence. Calling the sentence art would confuse esthetics with proof. The slogan still needs the premises that place it in the chain.

exercises.prompt: Build the description of an idea pulled out of the middle.

feedback.note: The sentence names the detachment: the idea is kept, and the premises that support it are gone. Calling that idea an axiom, or saying it needs no base, is the intrinsicism that treats a derivative claim as self-standing. Without those premises the idea is no longer functioning as part of the philosophy.

exercises.prompt: A lawyer quotes a principle of justice, rejects the ethics it comes from, and says the principle now rests on court custom. Has it been put back?

choices.text: Yes. Any substitute base is as good as the premises that supported it.
Yes. Custom is the social principle, so the chain is restored.
No. A foreign substitute is not the earlier principles that supported it.
No. Justice is the sort of idea that cannot be used in a court.

feedback.note: Putting a middle idea back means returning it to the earlier principles that support it, not swapping in a custom. Court custom is man-made and can contradict the principle, so it does not validate the idea it is asked to hold up. The error treats a replacement slogan as if it were the missing base. Justice can be used in a court when it is still tied to those premises.

exercises.prompt: Why can a middle idea, taken alone, not be validated?

choices.text: Validation would require the earlier principles that have been removed.
Only a laboratory can validate an idea, and philosophy has none.
A middle idea is a feeling, and feelings are neither true nor false.
Validation means counting the people who already like the wording.

feedback.note: Validation of a derivative idea shows that it follows from earlier principles and fits the facts those principles identify. Taken alone, the idea has nothing left to be checked against, because that base was removed. A vote does not validate it, and a feeling is not a middle idea's missing proof. The obstacle is the missing premises, not the absence of a laboratory.

exercises.prompt: What would validate a principle of justice that someone has been quoting by itself?

choices.text: Showing that it follows from what a person is, how one knows his actions, and what his life requires.
Noting that the word justice has an honorable sound.
Observing that the wording helped a speaker win an argument this week.
Learning that most listeners already agree with the sentence.

feedback.note: The principle is validated by being tied back to the earlier claims it rests on, about man, knowledge, and value. An honorable sound is intrinsicism, treating the words as if they carried the proof. Winning this week is pragmatism, which confuses a payoff with a derivation. A majority does not validate it, because numbers are not the premises it depends on.

exercises.prompt: Match each attempt to what it does for a detached middle idea.

pairs.left: Tie it back to the earlier principles it rests on
pairs.right: Validates it by restoring the base

pairs.left: Point out that the wording feels noble
pairs.right: Leaves it unvalidated

pairs.left: Cite a result that paid off this week
pairs.right: Offers a payoff in place of a proof

pairs.left: Count the people who already repeat it
pairs.right: Offers numbers in place of premises

feedback.note: Only the return to earlier principles validates a middle idea, because those principles are what it depends on. A noble feeling, a short-run payoff, and a head count leave it unvalidated. Each of those moves mistakes a side attraction for the base that was removed. The idea is not proved by being admired.

exercises.prompt: Complete the reason a detached middle idea cannot be proved.

parts.text: Taken alone, it has nothing left to
it.

feedback.note: The earlier principles are what could validate the idea, and detachment removes them. Reciting, advertising, or decorating the words does not put that base back, because none of those acts derives the idea from what exists and from how one knows. The gap is logical. Volume and ornament do not close it.

exercises.prompt: A student defends honesty by saying it feels clean, and he will not connect it to the role of reason in a human life. Why does that defense fail?

choices.text: A feeling is not the earlier principle that could validate the virtue.
A clean feeling is direct awareness of a moral fact, so the defense succeeds.
Virtues are valid precisely when nobody derives them.
Honesty is not a virtue and cannot appear in a chain of principles.

feedback.note: Honesty, as a virtue, rests on the need to use reason and to refuse to fake reality. A clean feeling does not establish that. It reports an estimate, and subjectivism treats the estimate as proof. The virtue is not valid by being left underived. The defense fails because the premises that could validate honesty were set aside.

exercises.prompt: Seeing that a detached slogan cannot be validated, a listener says every principle, including the axioms, is now unknowable. Which error is that?

choices.text: Skepticism: one unvalidated slogan is treated as the collapse of knowledge.
The right lesson: if a middle idea fails alone, nothing can be known.
Intrinsicism: the slogan is true because the words sit on the page.
Statism: only an official announcement can say which principles are knowable.

feedback.note: The slogan failed because it was detached, not because knowledge is impossible. Skepticism spreads that one failure across every principle, including axioms that do not depend on the missing middle. Intrinsicism would have called the slogan true by the mere fact that it was written, which is a different mistake. An official announcement would add an authority, not a validation.

exercises.prompt: Build the reason a middle idea cannot be validated once it is taken alone.

feedback.note: Nothing is left to validate the idea, because the earlier principles were removed with the detachment. A feeling or a vote cannot fill that place, since neither derives the idea from what exists and from how one knows. The sentence names the gap. It does not say the idea was never true when it still rested on its base.

exercises.prompt: Someone says rights need no earlier premises, because a right is as basic as the fact that existence exists. What is the mistake?

choices.text: A derivative principle is being treated as if it were an axiom.
Rights are correctly traced to what a person is and how his life must be lived.
Axioms are being denied their power to defeat an attempt to reject them.
Metaphysics is correctly placed after politics in the chain.

feedback.note: Existence exists is axiomatic, because an attempt to deny it already uses it. A right is a moral principle about action among people, and it rests on earlier claims about life, reason, and the person. Treating it as an axiom takes a middle idea as self-standing, with no method left that could validate it. The repair is to restore those premises, since a derivative principle does not become basic by being insisted on.

exercises.prompt: Why can that same detached idea not guide a concrete choice?

choices.text: Nothing is left to connect it to the facts of a particular case.
Concrete choices fall outside philosophy once the axioms are known.
A principle guides action only when it is chanted in a fixed wording.
Use requires the idea to contradict the premises it came from.

feedback.note: Application needs the wider view that says which facts matter and what kind of action follows. A detached idea has nothing left to make that connection, so it cannot guide the case. A chant does not restore the connection, and a contradiction would make the guidance worse. Concrete choices are where a principle still tied to its premises is used.

exercises.prompt: Two managers both say only "be rational," having dropped every account of reason, and they reach opposite hiring decisions. Why can the shared words not settle the case?

choices.text: Rationality forbids hiring, so both decisions are errors of the same kind.
The detached phrase no longer says which facts matter or what action follows.
Hiring is political, so an ethical phrase is not allowed to bear on it.
Opposite decisions prove that reason itself is a contradiction.

feedback.note: Inside the philosophy, reason means identifying and integrating the facts, including what each applicant has done. Detached, the words do not say which facts count, so opposite actions can wear the same label. That does not make reason contradictory. It shows there is nothing left to apply. Ethics does bear on hiring when the principle is still connected to those facts.

exercises.prompt: Match each result to the condition that produces it.

pairs.left: The idea cannot be shown to follow from anything
pairs.right: Nothing left to validate it

pairs.left: The idea cannot be carried into a particular decision
pairs.right: Nothing left to apply it

pairs.left: The idea is tied to earlier principles and used on the facts
pairs.right: Still inside the system

pairs.left: The wording is repeated while the case is ignored
pairs.right: A performance, rather than an application

feedback.note: Detachment does two kinds of damage. With the earlier principles gone, nothing is left to validate the idea, and nothing is left to apply it to a concrete choice. Repeating the words while ignoring the case is what people do once that connection is gone. An idea still inside the system can be checked and then used on the facts.

exercises.prompt: Complete the practical consequence of pulling an idea out of the middle.

parts.text: There is nothing left to apply it to a

feedback.note: Without the premises, the idea cannot be applied to a concrete choice. A louder slogan, a crowd, or a mood does not create the missing connection, because none of them identifies which facts of the case matter. The first gap was validation. The second is guidance of action, and it has the same cause.

exercises.prompt: A man says he will skip the question of truth and just apply a political slogan to a contract dispute. Why does the plan fail?

choices.text: With the premises gone, there is nothing left to apply to the dispute.
Application improves once the idea is freed from any claim to truth.
A contract is settled by whichever slogan is shorter.
Contracts are metaphysically given, so no principle applies to them.

feedback.note: Skipping validation does not unlock a use. The premises that would validate the slogan are the same premises that would say which facts of the dispute count and what action follows. Without them there is nothing left to apply. A contract is man-made, so it does call for principle, and shortness is not a standard. The plan treats use as a substitute for truth, which is pragmatism.

exercises.prompt: Which demand looks like a use of the idea and still is not one?

choices.text: Name the facts the full principle selects in this case, then act on that identification.
Recite the detached slogan over the case without identifying any fact it would select.
Restore the earlier premises, then judge the case by them.
Reject the slogan because it contradicts a known fact.

feedback.note: Reciting a detached slogan feels like application, but it identifies neither a fact nor an action, so it does not guide the choice. The other moves are different: one applies a principle that is still in the system, one restores the base first, and one drops a claim that contradicts a fact. The error in the recitation is to confuse emphasis with use.

exercises.prompt: Build the full consequence of taking a middle idea out of the system.

feedback.note: The detachment leaves nothing to validate the idea and nothing to apply it, because both jobs were done by the earlier principles. A chant or a vote does not restore either job. The sentence joins the two failures. It is not a reason to drop the idea in the place where it still rests on its base.

exercises.prompt: An editor accepts "judge by the facts," will not say what a fact is or how a mind knows one, and then says the maxim tells her to prefer the vivid draft. What is missing?

choices.text: Nothing. A vivid draft is a fact by virtue of being vivid.
Only a louder statement of the same maxim.
The premises that would validate the maxim and connect it to what the drafts are.
A vote of the readers, which would both validate and apply the maxim.

feedback.note: The maxim, inside the philosophy, rests on a view of facts and of knowledge. Detached, it cannot be validated, and it cannot select a draft, because vividness has not been identified as the relevant fact. Preferring the vivid draft smuggles in a feeling. A louder maxim or a readers' vote does not supply the missing premises. The same cut blocks the check and the choice.

exercises.prompt: What is a package deal, as against a real consequence or a later principle resting on an earlier one?

choices.text: Two claims treated as though they were a single claim.
Two claims judged separately, so a yes to one stays free of the other.
A principle together with the concrete action it requires here.
An earlier principle and the later principle that rests on it.

feedback.note: A package deal treats two claims as one, so that a yes or a no seems to cover both. Judging them separately is how the package is opened, not what the package is. A principle plus its action is an application, and an earlier principle with a later one is the chain of the philosophy. Those are real relations. A package deal is a pretended unity, usually hiding under one word.

exercises.prompt: Under the word selfishness, concern with one's own interests is treated as the same claim as brutality. What is that arrangement?

choices.text: One claim, because a single word can name only one thing.
A package deal: two claims glued together and treated as one.
A valid inference, because brutality follows from rational self-interest.
An axiom, because the word is widely used.

feedback.note: Rational self-interest and brutality are two claims. The package uses selfishness so that accepting the first seems to mean accepting the second. That is not a valid inference, because concern with one's own life and production does not entail brutality. Wide use does not make the glue an axiom. Opening the package starts by refusing to let the shared word do the arguing.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to the kind of object it is.

pairs.left: Concern with one's own interests, stated by itself
pairs.right: One claim, able to be judged alone

pairs.left: Brutality, stated by itself
pairs.right: A second claim, not a consequence of the first

pairs.left: Both, offered as the single meaning of one word
pairs.right: A package deal

pairs.left: A conclusion that really follows from a stated premise
pairs.right: A consequence, not a package

feedback.note: A package deal is two claims treated as one. Concern with one's own interests is one claim, and brutality is another; the second does not follow merely because a word covers both. A real consequence is different, because there the second claim follows and accepting the first commits you to it. The error is the fake unity, not every relation between two sentences.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition of a package deal.

parts.text: A package deal treats two claims as

feedback.note: The definition says two claims are treated as one, which is why a single answer seems to dispose of both. Calling them opposites would describe a different structure. Calling them axioms or facts would promote the package into the base of knowledge, because those are not what the glue created. The repair is to name each claim. A new label for the pair would leave the fake unity in place.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a real consequence, not a package deal?

choices.text: Selfishness means rational self-interest, and therefore it means brutality.
A right sanctions one's own action, and therefore it claims another person's product.
Freedom from initiated force rules out a law that initiates force.
A concession on a detail is the same act as surrendering a basic principle.

feedback.note: If freedom is the absence of initiated force, then a law that initiates force contradicts it. That second clause follows, so it is a consequence. The other three are packages, because selfishness glues rational self-interest to brutality, right glues a sanction of one's own action to a claim on someone else's product, and compromise glues a trade about a non-essential to a surrender of principle. A yes to a real principle commits you to its consequence, not to a smuggled claim.

exercises.prompt: Why is it not enough to say that two ideas in one sentence are a package deal?

choices.text: A package deal is two claims treated as one, not the mere sharing of a sentence.
Package deals occur only in words of one syllable.
Any two claims in one sentence really are a single claim.
Only a revelation can identify the join between two claims.

feedback.note: Sharing a sentence is not the error. The error is treating two claims that should be judged apart as if they were a single claim. One principle can need two clauses that belong together, and a conclusion can share a sentence with its premise. Counting syllables is irrelevant, and mysticism is not required, because you can see the join by asking whether accepting one claim actually commits you to the other.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that defines a package deal and keeps it distinct from a proof.

feedback.note: A package deal treats two claims as one, so a verdict on the pair replaces two judgments. Calling that treatment a proof, or an axiom, inflates the glue into knowledge. The definition does not say that related claims are always a package. A real consequence still follows from its premise, and that relation is a different thing.

exercises.prompt: The trader principle says: give value for value, and do not seek the unearned. Someone calls it a package deal because it has two clauses. Is it one?

choices.text: Yes. Two clauses are always two claims glued together by grammar.
No. The two clauses state one principle, and the second forbids a breach of the first.
Yes. Trade is a ritual, so any wording of it is a package.
No. Package deals occur only in politics, never in ethics.

feedback.note: Giving value for value and refusing the unearned are one principle stated in two clauses. The second clause rules out a breach of the first; it is not a stranger claim smuggled in by a word. Grammar does not create a package, and the error is not confined to politics. Calling trade a ritual confuses this with a different failure. A package would glue claims that do not belong as one, such as self-interest and brutality.

exercises.prompt: What usually glues the two claims of a package deal into an apparent single claim?

choices.text: A derivation that really shows the second claim follows from the first.
A single word, used so that both claims seem to be its meaning.
A laboratory result that confirms both claims at once.
An axiom that makes the two claims identical.

feedback.note: The glue is usually a single word. Selfishness, freedom, right, and compromise are used so that two different claims seem to be one meaning. A derivation in which the second claim really follows is an argument, not glue, because a real derivation does not hide a join. A laboratory result or an axiom would be evidence or a base. Finding the word locates the place where the two claims were fused.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to the two claims it is used to glue together.

pairs.left: Selfishness
pairs.right: Rational self-interest glued to brutality

pairs.left: Freedom
pairs.right: Absence of initiated force glued to a license to initiate force

pairs.left: Right
pairs.right: A sanction of one's own action glued to a claim on another's product

pairs.left: Compromise
pairs.right: A trade about non-essentials glued to surrender of a basic principle

feedback.note: Each word is glue when it fuses two claims that have to be judged apart. Selfishness is not brutality. Freedom from initiated force is not a license to start it. A sanction of one's own action is not a claim on another person's product. A trade about a non-essential is not a surrender of principle. The match names the join. It does not yet judge either claim.

exercises.prompt: In the attack "selfishness is brutality," which item is the glue?

choices.text: The word selfishness, used to make rational self-interest and brutality seem identical.
Brutality itself, which is the whole meaning of rational self-interest.
A derivation showing that robbery follows from production.
The principle that a person is an end in himself.

feedback.note: The glue is the word selfishness. It is being used so that concern with one's own interests and brutality seem to be one claim. They are not, and robbery does not follow from production. The principle that a person is an end in himself is an ethical premise, not the glue in this attack. Once the word is spotted, each claim can be named on its own.

exercises.prompt: Complete the account of how a package deal is held shut.

parts.text: The glue is usually a single

feedback.note: A single word is what usually glues the claims, because one label feels like one meaning. A fact, an axiom, or a proof would be a reason, and a reason is not hidden glue. If a proof were present, the second claim would follow and there would be no package to open. The method starts by naming the word that is doing the fusing.

exercises.prompt: A negotiator says, "You reject compromise, so you reject every mutual concession, including a change in the delivery hour." Which word is the glue?

choices.text: Delivery, fusing a clock reading to the existence of contracts.
Reject, fusing a moral no to a refusal to look at any detail.
Compromise, fusing a trade about a non-essential to a surrender of basic principle.
Hour, fusing the passage of time to the law of identity.

feedback.note: Compromise is the glue. It is used so that a trade about a non-essential, here the delivery hour, seems identical to surrendering a basic principle. Rejecting the surrender does not reject the trade. Delivery and hour name the detail; they do not fuse the two claims. The error lets one word carry a concession on a particular and a betrayal of principle as if they were the same act.

exercises.prompt: Someone hears the defined term initiated force and says it is a package deal because it is a short phrase. What is missed?

choices.text: A defined term is glue whenever it is short.
A word is glue only when it treats two claims as one. A term that names one fact is not glue.
Initiated force names two claims: any force, and the existence of consciousness.
Definitions are revelations, so every term hides a package.

feedback.note: Glue is a use, not a length. Initiated force names one fact: someone started the use of physical compulsion. It does not fuse that fact with a second, unrelated claim. Calling every short term a package would make definition impossible. Freedom is glue when it fuses the absence of initiated force with a license to initiate force. The same sound, used to name only the first claim, is not glue.

exercises.prompt: Build the line that names the usual glue.

feedback.note: The glue is usually a single word, which is why the two claims feel like one meaning. A valid proof would show that the second claim follows, and an axiom would be a base rather than a hiding place. Substituting either one changes the diagnosis, because neither one is the word that hides the join. The next step is to open that word and name the claims it covered.

exercises.prompt: An editorial says freedom means no initiated force and also means the license to seize, and that you cannot accept one without the other. What is the word freedom doing there?

choices.text: Working as a precise term, because both clauses were printed.
Working as glue: one word treats the absence of initiated force and the license to initiate it as one claim.
Stating an axiom, because an editorial reports a basic metaphysical fact.
Serving as a script that tells the reader which sentence to recite.

feedback.note: Freedom is glue in that editorial because one word is made to cover the absence of initiated force and the license to initiate force, as if they were a single meaning. Printing both clauses displays the package; it does not make them one fact. The word is not an axiom and not a script. A precise use would name only the absence of initiated force, and a license to seize would then stand as a contradiction of it.

exercises.prompt: You have found the word that glues a package. What does opening the package require first?

choices.text: Name each claim separately.
Accept both claims, because they shared a word.
Reject both claims, because the word was tainted.
Replace both claims with a feeling about the word.

feedback.note: Opening the package means naming each claim, so that each can be looked at alone. Accepting both repeats the package. Rejecting both lets the glue decide a double no, which is still one verdict covering two claims. A feeling about the word is subjectivism, because a feeling does not name either claim. Naming is not yet the judgment, but without the names there is nothing distinct to judge.

exercises.prompt: Open the package hidden in a sloppy use of freedom. What are the two claims, named apart?

choices.text: The absence of initiated force, and the license to initiate force.
The absence of initiated force, stated twice in different tones.
A claim on another person's product, and a tax on unused land.
A change in the delivery hour, and a surrender of metaphysics.

feedback.note: Named apart, the claims are the absence of initiated force and the license to initiate force. They are not one claim in two tones, because the second contradicts the first. A claim on another person's product belongs to the package under right. A delivery hour belongs under compromise. Putting those pairs here would misname the freedom package rather than open it.

exercises.prompt: Match each concrete act to the claim it actually is, once the package is opened.

pairs.left: Keeping the product of your own work
pairs.right: A sanction of one's own action

pairs.left: Taking the product of someone else's work
pairs.right: A claim on another person's product

pairs.left: Changing a delivery hour, with the principle intact
pairs.right: A trade about a non-essential

pairs.left: Dropping the ban on initiated force to win a vote
pairs.right: A surrender of a basic principle

feedback.note: Opening a package means stating each claim in words that do not smuggle the other. Keeping what you produced is a sanction of your own action, while taking what someone else produced is a different claim. A change of hour, with the principle intact, is a trade about a non-essential. Dropping the ban on initiated force is a surrender of principle, because it is not a detail of scheduling.

exercises.prompt: Complete the first step in opening a package.

parts.text: Name each
by itself.

feedback.note: What you name is each claim, because the package was two claims treated as one. A slogan, a crowd, or a gesture is not the content hidden by the glue. Until each claim is stated in its own words, the word is still doing the thinking. Naming them does not yet mean that either one has been accepted or rejected.

exercises.prompt: A platform demands a right to a house produced by someone else. Name the two claims inside that use of right.

choices.text: A sanction of the producer's own action, and a claim on that other person's product.
Two sanctions of the same action, differing only in emphasis.
A trade about the paint color, and a trade about the delivery date.
Brutality, and a second brutality under another name.

feedback.note: The word right is hiding a sanction of one's own action and a claim on another person's product. A house someone else produced is the second claim, not another way of sanctioning the producer's action. Paint and delivery belong to a compromise package, and brutality belongs to the selfishness package, because each package has its own pair. Naming this pair is what makes a separate judgment possible.

exercises.prompt: After naming both claims, a student says he has already accepted the first and rejected the second. What has he confused?

choices.text: Naming with judging. The names make two judgments possible; they are not those judgments.
An axiom with a theorem. The first claim he names is always axiomatic.
Metaphysics with esthetics, because both use the word value.
A script with a ritual, because both were mentioned in the naming.

feedback.note: Naming each claim opens the package and stops there. Judging is a further act: you decide, of each claim, whether it stands. He skipped that act and treated the order of the names as a verdict. The first claim is not automatically an axiom. The confusion is not about esthetics, and it is not about scripts. It is the preparation for a judgment treated as the judgment itself.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction that opens a package deal.

feedback.note: The instruction is to name each claim separately from the other, which breaks the fake unity. Treating them as one claim would shut the package again, and naming them by the glue word would leave the word in charge. Naming is the step that makes two later answers possible. It does not itself deliver those answers.

exercises.prompt: Asked to open the right package, a writer says a claim on another person's product just is a sanction of one's own action, in different words. What did he fail to do?

choices.text: He failed to name two claims, and restated the package as if it were a definition.
He named them apart, because the sentence was longer than the original word.
He validated the claim by deriving it from metaphysics.
He applied justice to the facts of a particular dispute.

feedback.note: A sanction of one's own action is not a claim on another person's product, so the paraphrase is false. He kept the package by redescribing it, instead of naming each claim in words that leave the other out. Length does not open a package. He did not derive the claim from metaphysics, and he did not apply it to a dispute. The failure is at the naming step, so the later judgment never gets two objects.

exercises.prompt: The two claims have been named. What follows from a yes given to one of them?

choices.text: It is a yes to the other as well, because they were once glued.
It is a yes to that claim alone. The other claim still has to be judged.
It cancels identity for both claims.
It is meaningless, because only whole packages can be accepted or rejected.

feedback.note: A yes to one claim is not a yes to the other. The glue made them look like a single item; once they are named, each judgment stands alone. Identity is respected by judging them separately, because each claim is what it is. The view that only whole packages can be judged is the package defending itself. The answers are allowed to diverge.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about self-interest in production and self-interest in robbery?
exercises.quote: There is a fundamental moral difference between a man who sees his self-interest in production and a man who sees it in robbery.

choices.text: There is a fundamental moral difference between them.
They are the same moral claim under two names.
Robbery is a slower form of production.
The difference depends on which one a person prefers that day.

feedback.quote: There is a fundamental moral difference between a man who sees his self-interest in production and a man who sees it in robbery.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "Introduction," The Virtue of Selfishness, ix
feedback.note: The passage establishes a fundamental moral difference between seeing one's interest in production and seeing it in robbery. Treating them as one claim is the selfishness package, which glues rational self-interest to brutality. Preference does not create the difference; that would be subjectivism. A yes to productive self-interest therefore does not count as a yes to robbery.

exercises.prompt: Match each yes to the further yes it does not include.

pairs.left: Yes to rational self-interest
pairs.right: Not a yes to brutality

pairs.left: Yes to freedom from initiated force
pairs.right: Not a yes to a license to initiate force

pairs.left: Yes to a sanction of one's own action
pairs.right: Not a yes to a claim on another's product

pairs.left: Yes to a trade about a non-essential
pairs.right: Not a yes to surrendering a basic principle

feedback.note: Each yes stops at the claim that was judged. Rational self-interest does not include brutality. Freedom from initiated force does not include a license to start force. A sanction of one's own action does not include a claim on another person's product. A trade about a non-essential does not include surrendering a principle. The package says one yes is both. Judging them alone lets the answers diverge.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule for a judgment inside an opened package.

parts.text: A yes to one claim is not a yes to the

feedback.note: A yes to one claim is not a yes to the other, because they were two claims even while a word glued them. The glue, a crowd, or a ritual cannot turn the first yes into the second. Hearing a defense of self-interest as a defense of brutality, or a defense of rights as a demand for someone else's product, is obedience to the package. The second claim stays open until it is judged by itself.

exercises.prompt: Someone says brutality is evil, and therefore rational self-interest is evil. What has the package been allowed to do?

choices.text: Force a no to both claims, as if rejecting brutality rejected self-interest.
Judge each claim on its own and reject only the one that deserves it.
Derive brutality from giving value for value, as a real consequence.
Restore an ethical principle to the metaphysics it rests on.

feedback.note: Rejecting brutality does not decide the other claim. The package is what makes the two nos seem compulsory. Judged alone, brutality is evil and rational self-interest is not, so the answers diverge. This is not a consequence of giving value for value, and it is not a return to metaphysics. The error is a double verdict: a no to one claim was spent as a no to the other.

exercises.prompt: You affirm a person's right to act and to keep what that action produces. A neighbor says you have therefore affirmed his right to take the product. What is the answer?

choices.text: He is right. A right is a claim on someone else's goods.
A yes to the sanction of one's own action is not a yes to a claim on another person's product.
Both claims should be rejected, because the word right was used.
The taking is a non-essential, so a compromise requires handing the product over.

feedback.note: The right that was affirmed sanctions one's own action, including keeping what one produced. A claim to take another person's product is a different claim, and it contradicts the first, because the producer has the sanction of his own action. Rejecting both because of the word, or calling the seizure a compromise on a non-essential, still treats the package as one item. The yes does not travel to the smuggled claim.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule that stops one answer from counting twice.

feedback.note: A yes to one claim is not a yes to the other. Extending it to both claims is the package deal, and extending it to the glue lets the word decide.
