The rule makes the examples workable, because self-interest does not include brutality, freedom from initiated force does not include a license to start it, a right does not include a claim on another's product, and a concession on a detail does not include a surrendered principle.

exercises.prompt: A colleague will not change a meeting time. He says any concession surrenders a basic principle. No principle is at stake in the hour. What is the error?

choices.text: There is no error. Every concession is a surrender of principle.
He spends a no to surrendering a principle as a no to a trade about a non-essential.
He is applying justice, because an hour is another person's product.
He is right because the hour was metaphysically fixed.

feedback.note: A trade about a non-essential and a surrender of a basic principle are different claims, and compromise is the word that glues them. He rejects the surrender, which is right, and then spends that no on the meeting time, which does not follow. The hour is not another person's product, and it is not metaphysically fixed. A yes to the small trade can stand with a no to betraying a principle. He will not let those answers diverge.

exercises.prompt: What should replace a package deal when you are ready to judge it?

choices.text: One question, using the glue-word, so one answer covers both claims.
Two questions, one for each claim, answered one at a time.
A ritual recitation of the word, with no question asked.
A vote on how the word makes the listeners feel.

feedback.note: The package becomes two questions, because there were two claims. One question phrased with the glue-word puts the package back together and demands a single answer. A recitation is a ritual, and a vote on a feeling is subjectivism. Asking the questions one at a time lets a yes to one claim stand without becoming a yes to the other. Each question should name a claim, not the glue.

exercises.prompt: The packaged question is whether selfishness is good. Which pair replaces it?

choices.text: Is concern with one's own rational interests good? Is brutality good?
Is selfishness good, asked slowly? Is selfishness good, asked loudly?
Does the majority dislike the word? Does the word sound harsh?
Is every concession a surrender? Is every right a claim on a product?

feedback.note: The two questions name the claims that selfishness glued, because those claims are rational self-interest and brutality. They can be answered one at a time, and the answers need not match. Repeating the packaged question at any volume keeps the glue. A poll about tone is subjectivism. Questions about concession and about rights belong to other packages, so they would misname this one.

exercises.prompt: Match each glue-word to the pair of questions that replaces it.

pairs.left: Selfishness
pairs.right: Is rational self-interest good, and is brutality good?

pairs.left: Freedom
pairs.right: Does this bar initiated force, and does it license initiating force?

pairs.left: Right
pairs.right: Does this sanction one's own action, and does it claim another's product?

pairs.left: Compromise
pairs.right: Is this a trade about a non-essential, and is it a surrender of principle?

feedback.note: Each pair splits one word into the two claims it hid. Selfishness divides into rational self-interest and brutality. Freedom divides into a bar on initiated force and a license to initiate it. Right divides into a sanction of one's own action and a claim on another's product. Compromise divides into a trade about a non-essential and a surrender of principle. One answer to the glue-word cannot do that work, because the pair is two judgments.

exercises.prompt: Complete the method that replaces a package deal.

parts.text: Ask two questions, and answer them

feedback.note: The questions have to be answered one at a time, because a single verdict would rebuild the package. Applause and a gesture do not answer either question; they substitute a reaction for a judgment. Answering as one verdict is the error being removed. The two answers are allowed to differ. Yes to rational self-interest and no to brutality is a completed use of the method.

exercises.prompt: A statute is praised as freedom because it lets one group seize another's press. Which pair of answers fits the two freedom questions?

choices.text: It does not leave people free of initiated force, and it does license that force.
It leaves people free of initiated force, and the seizure is not force.
It is a trade about a non-essential, and no principle is involved.
It sanctions the printers' own action and claims nothing they produced.

feedback.note: The two questions ask whether the statute bars initiated force and whether it licenses initiating force. Seizing a press is initiated force, so the statute fails the first and commits the second. Calling the seizure freedom uses the glue. It is not a trade about a non-essential, and it does not sanction the printers' own action. It is a claim on their product carried out by force. The pair of answers keeps the word from swallowing those facts.

exercises.prompt: A bill calls a subsidy, paid out of the producers' goods, a right. What do the two right questions show?

choices.text: It sanctions the recipients' own production, and it takes nothing of theirs.
It does not sanction the recipients' own action. It claims another person's product.
Both questions are improper, because a statute is metaphysically given.
It is freedom, because the recipients are less constrained than before.

feedback.note: The two questions ask whether the bill sanctions a person's own action and whether it claims another person's product. A subsidy paid from the producers' goods is the second, and it is not the first: the recipients are not being left free in an action of producing those goods. Calling it freedom confuses this package with the force package. A statute is man-made, so it is not a metaphysically given fact that questions may not touch.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction that replaces the packaged question.

feedback.note: Ask two questions and answer each by itself. One glued question restores the package, and one feeling is subjectivism standing in for both judgments. The instruction is the method of the correction, because you find the word, name the claims, and refuse to let one answer count as the other. It works the same way for selfishness, freedom, right, and compromise.

exercises.prompt: A council calls the seizure of a workshop both a right and a compromise with the owner. Which reading opens both packages?

choices.text: It is a right because the council used the word, and a compromise because the owner was mentioned.
It claims another's product rather than sanctioning his action, and it surrenders the principle of rights rather than trading a non-essential.
It is freedom from force, and therefore a form of rational self-interest, so both words are precise.
It is a ritual gesture, so neither word needs to be opened.

feedback.note: Right splits into a sanction of one's own action and a claim on another's product; this seizure is the second. Compromise splits into a trade about a non-essential and a surrender of a basic principle; seizing the workshop surrenders the principle of rights. Mentioning the owner does not create a trade, and freedom does not rename the seizure. The council stacked two packages. Opening them means asking both pairs, rather than saluting either label.

exercises.prompt: What counts as a clash between a conclusion and the world?

choices.text: A conclusion that does not fit a known fact.
Two feelings that pull in different directions.
A fact you dislike, while your conclusion already agrees with it.
Two metaphysically given facts that contradict each other.

feedback.note: A clash is a conclusion that does not fit a known fact. Feelings can conflict without any conclusion having been checked against the world. Disliking a fact is not a clash while the conclusion still agrees with it. Two metaphysically given facts do not contradict each other, because a contradiction is an error in thinking. The clash is that error, at the point where a conclusion and a fact will not both stand.

exercises.prompt: You know the road is closed. Your conclusion is that you will drive it at noon. Where is the clash?

choices.text: There is none, because a plan is itself a fact about the road.
The conclusion does not fit the known fact that the road is closed.
The fact fails to fit your wish, so the fact is the error.
The road contradicts itself, because a closed road cannot be a road.

feedback.note: The known fact is that the road is closed, and the conclusion that you will drive it does not fit that fact. A plan is not a rival fact that outranks the closing. Treating the fact as the error reverses the clash. Identity has not failed: a closed road is a closed road. The clash is in the conclusion. Seeing that mismatch comes before asking which premise produced the plan.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its role when a conclusion meets a fact.

pairs.left: The conclusion
pairs.right: The claim that may fail to fit

pairs.left: The known fact
pairs.right: What the conclusion has to fit

pairs.left: The clash
pairs.right: The conclusion's failure to fit the fact

pairs.left: A wish that the fact were otherwise
pairs.right: Not a clash, unless a conclusion denies the fact

feedback.note: The conclusion is what can fail, and the known fact is what it has to fit. The clash is that failure, not the unpleasantness of the fact. A wish that things were otherwise is not yet a clash, because a wish is not a conclusion. It becomes part of one only if you conclude, against the fact, that things are as you wish. These roles keep you from editing the fact to soothe the conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition of this kind of clash.

parts.text: A clash is a conclusion that does not fit a known

feedback.note: The thing a conclusion must fit is a known fact. A mood, a vote, or a style can be reported, but none of them is the standard the conclusion is checked against. Subjectivism would put the mood in the fact's place, and a vote would put numbers there. If the conclusion does not fit the fact, you have a clash. You do not have a choice of wording.

exercises.prompt: Which situation is not a clash between a conclusion and a known fact?

choices.text: The scale reads ten pounds. The conclusion says the parcel weighs thirty.
The witness was elsewhere. The conclusion says he saw the event.
You wish the scale read thirty, and your conclusion still says ten, matching the scale.
The reagent did not change color. The conclusion says it did.

feedback.note: A wish that the scale read otherwise is not a clash while the conclusion still matches the known fact. The other three are clashes: the conclusion denies the scale, the witness's location, or the reagent. Disliking a fact is a different thing from contradicting it. The method begins only when a conclusion and a known fact will not both stand, which is why the mere wish is set aside.

exercises.prompt: Someone says the clash proves that reality contradicts itself. What is the mistake?

choices.text: A clash is a fault in a conclusion, not a feature of the facts.
He is right, because two reports are two realities.
He is right whenever the person who concluded was sincere.
A fact is only another conclusion, so there is no fact in the clash.

feedback.note: Reality does not contradict itself. A contradiction is an error in thinking, and this clash is that kind of error: the conclusion does not fit a known fact. Sincerity does not move the fault into the world, and a second report does not create a second reality. Treating the fact as just another conclusion would leave nothing for a conclusion to be checked against. The fact stays, and the conclusion is what the clash puts in question.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that defines a clash between a conclusion and a fact.

feedback.note: A clash is a conclusion that does not fit a known fact. A disliked fact, while the conclusion still agrees with it, is not that mismatch. Two realities would abandon identity. The definition puts the fault on the conclusion's side. It does not yet name the premise to inspect. It fixes what the mismatch is, so the later steps have an object.

exercises.prompt: A new measurement contradicts your conclusion. You say there is no clash yet, because you have not chosen to call it a contradiction. Are you right?

choices.text: Yes. A clash exists only after you announce it.
No. The clash is the mismatch with the known fact, whether or not you have named it.
Yes. A measurement is a wish written with decimal points.
No. Every measurement abolishes the principle of identity.

feedback.note: The clash is the conclusion's failure to fit a known fact, and the measurement is that fact. Declining to call it a contradiction does not remove the mismatch. Subjectivism is what treats the naming, or the measurement, as optional feeling. Identity is not abolished by a measurement; a measurement is an identification. The method starts when the mismatch is admitted, not when a label feels comfortable.

exercises.prompt: A conclusion clashes with a known fact. Which side has to give?

choices.text: The fact, rewritten until the conclusion sits comfortably.
The conclusion. The fact holds.
Both, averaged into a view that offends neither side.
Neither. A clash is a permanent feature of knowledge.

feedback.note: The fact holds, and the clashing conclusion is the side that has to give. Rewriting the fact to save the conclusion reverses that. An average fakes both the fact and the conclusion, because it is a diplomatic third thing rather than respect for what is known. A clash signals that the conclusion, or the premise behind it, is wrong. The method keeps the fact.

exercises.prompt: A beam measures short of the length the plan requires. The planner writes that for the project's purposes it is long enough, and he keeps the plan. What did he do to the fact?

choices.text: He kept it, because a project's purposes are a measurement.
He rewrote it so the conclusion could stand.
He traced the conclusion to the premise that produced it.
He replaced a faulty premise with one that fits the measurement.

feedback.note: The measurement is the known fact, and it holds. Saying that the beam is long enough for the project's purposes rewrites that fact so the plan can survive. He did not trace the conclusion to a premise, and he did not replace one. The appeal to purposes is pragmatism, because the fact is adjusted to what the plan needs. The method keeps the fact and judges the plan against it.

exercises.prompt: Match each response to the status it gives the fact.

pairs.left: Keep the measurement and drop the conclusion that denies it
pairs.right: The fact holds

pairs.left: Restate the measurement until it agrees with the plan
pairs.right: The fact is rewritten

pairs.left: Call the measurement a feeling about the metal
pairs.right: The fact is replaced by a feeling

pairs.left: Say the length cannot be known as it is
pairs.right: The fact is set aside as unknowable

feedback.note: The fact holds, so the measurement stays and the clashing conclusion gives. Restating the measurement to suit the plan rewrites the fact. Calling it a feeling is subjectivism. Saying the length cannot be known as it is sets the fact aside, which is the skeptical or Kantian move, instead of checking the conclusion against it. All three errors save the conclusion by touching the fact, because none of them lets the fact hold.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule that decides which side of a clash survives.

parts.text: When a conclusion clashes with a known fact, the fact

feedback.note: The fact holds. Yielding, taking a vote, or fading would let the conclusion edit what is known. A vote is not a measurement, and a fade is only a softer rewrite. The rule is one-sided because the world does not make room for a conclusion that misses it. What can change is the conclusion, and later the premise that produced it.

exercises.prompt: A theorist says the mind's forms structure experience, so the measurement is not a fact about the beam as it is, and the plan may stand. What is the error?

choices.text: He keeps the fact and drops the plan.
He treats the clash as unknowable, and the conclusion is shielded from the fact.
He traces the plan to the premise that the beam was long enough.
He distinguishes a given length from a man-made plan.

feedback.note: This is the Kantian move: the mind's forms structure experience, so we do not know the beam as it is, and a measurement never qualifies as the fact that could refute a plan. The clash is declared unknowable and the conclusion is safe. That shields the conclusion by retiring the fact. The length holds whether or not a plan likes it, because the plan, not the beam, is what has to be checked.

exercises.prompt: The planner says the conclusion works for the schedule, so the measurement can be treated as flexible. Which error is that?

choices.text: Pragmatism: what works for the plan is allowed to rewrite the fact.
A proper check, because a schedule is evidence about the beam.
Causality: a plan causes a beam to match the length the plan names.
Hierarchy: a schedule rests on a measurement by coming before it.

feedback.note: Pragmatism takes truth to be what works, here what works for the schedule, and then bends the measurement. A schedule is not evidence about the beam's length. The measurement is. Causality does not let a plan rewrite an entity's attribute, and the right hierarchy puts the measurement ahead of the conclusion that uses it. The fact holds. A useful schedule that contradicts it is not knowledge.

exercises.prompt: Build the rule for the side of the clash that stands.

feedback.note: The fact holds and the conclusion gives way. Rewriting the fact, or putting it to a vote, saves the conclusion by attacking the thing that showed it to be wrong. The sentence does not say to discard every other idea you hold. It says this conclusion cannot stand against this fact. The next work is to find the premise that produced the conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Rather than drop a conclusion that contradicts a fact, a person says he never reached it, though his plan still depends on it. What is he doing?

choices.text: Letting the fact hold and withdrawing the conclusion.
Hiding the clash, while still using the conclusion the fact refutes.
Replacing the premise so the new conclusion fits the fact.
Showing that the fact was misreported.

feedback.note: Saying the conclusion was never reached, while the plan still depends on it, hides the clash instead of letting the conclusion give. The fact holds either way. He has not replaced a premise, and he has not shown that the fact was misreported. The error is a verbal retreat that leaves the contradicted conclusion in operation. The method requires the opposite: keep the fact, and actually give up the conclusion that will not fit it.

exercises.prompt: The fact holds, and the conclusion clashes with it. What is the next step?

choices.text: Trace the conclusion to the premise that produced it.
Rewrite the fact in milder language.
Discard every idea you hold, beginning with the axioms.
Repeat the conclusion until it feels compatible with the fact.

feedback.note: The next step is to trace the conclusion to the premise that produced it, because a conclusion does not appear from nowhere. Rewriting the fact was already ruled out: the fact holds. Discarding every idea, including the axioms, is skepticism, spreading one clash across knowledge. Repetition changes nothing. The premise you want is the claim that, together with the other beliefs in use, yielded this conclusion.

exercises.prompt: The conclusion was that the plan cannot fail. It came from the premise that a sincere plan succeeds. The plan failed. Which claim do you trace?

choices.text: The premise that a sincere plan succeeds.
The claim that plans are human actions, which did not generate the guarantee.
The axiom that existence exists, because every error refutes an axiom.
The fact that the planners had names, which is beside the failure.

feedback.note: The conclusion that the plan could not fail was produced by the premise that a sincere plan succeeds. That is the premise to trace. Plans can be human actions, and planners can have names, without either claim generating the guarantee. Existence exists is not refuted by a failed plan. Tracing means finding the producing premise, not blaming the nearest truth or the widest axiom.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its role in the trace.

pairs.left: The failed conclusion
pairs.right: What you trace backward from

pairs.left: The producing premise
pairs.right: The earlier claim that yielded the conclusion

pairs.left: A true belief that did no work in the inference
pairs.right: Not the premise the trace is after

pairs.left: The known fact
pairs.right: The reason the conclusion cannot stand

feedback.note: You start from the conclusion that clashes and move back to the premise that produced it. A true belief that played no role in the inference is not that premise, so the trace is not a license to indict every nearby sentence. The known fact is why the conclusion cannot stand. Mixing these roles rewrites the fact or punishes an idea that did not generate the error, because the fact is not itself the premise.

exercises.prompt: Complete the instruction for tracing a conclusion that clashes with a fact.

parts.text: Trace the conclusion to the
that produced it.

feedback.note: What you trace is the premise that produced the conclusion, not the fact the conclusion failed to fit. The fact holds and is not the thing under indictment. An audience or a gesture did not do the logical work, and a mood is not a premise either, because the premise is the claim that, inside the inference, yielded the conclusion. Name that claim.

exercises.prompt: The conclusion was badly wanted. A friend says the premise was therefore the wanting. What is wrong with that trace?

choices.text: Nothing. An emotion is the cognition that produces a conclusion.
Wanting is not the premise. The premise is the claim that did the logical work.
The wanting refutes the known fact.
A strong want is an axiom, so the trace properly stops there.

feedback.note: An emotion is not a tool of cognition, and it is not the premise that produced the conclusion. The wanting may explain why the error was attractive. It does not identify the claim that yielded the conclusion. Treating the want as an axiom, or as something that refutes the fact, confuses a motive with an inference. A motive can sit beside a true premise or a false one, so it does not pick out which claim did the work.

exercises.prompt: The faulty conclusion came from the claim that confidence guarantees the result. A critic traces it instead to the claim that people sometimes study, which was not used. What is the error?

choices.text: He traced the conclusion to the premise that produced it.
He traced it to a claim that did not produce it, because that claim was easier to attack.
He kept the fact and dropped the contradicted conclusion.
He replaced the guarantee with a demand that the result be checked.

feedback.note: The producing premise is that confidence guarantees the result. The claim that people sometimes study may be true, and it did not yield the conclusion, so the trace missed. Attacking an easier nearby sentence leaves the real premise in place. That attack is not the method, because the method keeps the fact, drops the contradicted conclusion, and replaces the guarantee that produced it.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction for the backward step.

feedback.note: Trace the conclusion to the premise that produced it. A wish is not that premise, and neither is the set of every axiom, because one bad inference does not put the base of knowledge on trial. Those substitutes either psychologize the error or spread it into skepticism. The instruction is narrow on purpose. Find the claim that did the work.

exercises.prompt: From "whoever agrees with me is honest" and "he agreed with me," you concluded that he is honest. He did agree, and he falsified the report. Which premise do you trace?

choices.text: That he agreed, because the sentence mentions him.
That whoever agrees with you is honest, because that claim turned agreement into honesty.
Both equally, because every premise mentioned near a conclusion is guilty.
That he falsified the report, because the fact is the premise that failed.

feedback.note: The agreement can be a fact and still not be the error. The premise that produced the conclusion is the general claim that agreement proves honesty. The falsification is the known fact the conclusion clashed with, not a premise in the inference. Tracing both equally would discard a true particular along with a false general, which is more than the clash requires, because you follow the claim that did the logical work.

exercises.prompt: You have found the premise that produced the clashing conclusion. What does inspecting it mean?

choices.text: Check that premise against the fact, and see whether it can still stand.
Shield it, because the conclusion was wanted.
Rewrite the fact so the premise no longer has to face it.
Discard every idea you hold, in case the failure is total.

feedback.note: Inspecting means checking the producing premise against the fact. Shielding it because the conclusion was wanted treats a desire as evidence. Rewriting the fact puts the fact on trial, which reverses the clash. Discarding every idea is skepticism, a refusal to look at this premise in particular. The inspection asks one question: given the fact that holds, can this premise still be true?

exercises.prompt: Which response inspects the premise, rather than avoiding the inspection?

choices.text: The conclusion matters too much, so leave the premise alone.
So much failed that existence itself is now in doubt.
Change the measurement until the premise fits it.
Does this premise still stand, given the fact that holds?

feedback.note: The inspecting question asks whether the premise stands given the fact. Protecting it for the sake of a wanted conclusion shields it. Doubting existence because one premise failed discards every idea, not this one. Changing the measurement rewrites the fact. All three avoid the inspection while looking severe. The actual check is narrower: the fact stays, and this premise is what has to meet it.

exercises.prompt: Match each response to the error or the act it is.

pairs.left: Edit the fact so the premise survives
pairs.right: Rewriting the fact

pairs.left: Throw out the axioms along with the bad premise
pairs.right: Discarding every idea one holds

pairs.left: Keep the premise because the conclusion was wanted
pairs.right: Shielding the premise

pairs.left: Ask whether the premise fits the fact that holds
pairs.right: Inspecting the premise

feedback.note: Rewriting the fact, discarding every idea, and shielding the premise are three ways of not inspecting. They feel different: one is diplomatic, one is despairing, and one is loyal to a wanted conclusion. All three leave the producing premise untested. Inspection is the remaining move, because it checks that premise against the fact and allows the answer to be no.

exercises.prompt: Complete the instruction for the premise you have traced.

parts.text: Check that premise against the

feedback.note: The premise is checked against the fact, because the fact holds and the conclusion failed to fit it. A wish, a vote, or a slogan cannot be the standard of that check. Using them shields the premise or replaces the standard. The drama of the wanted conclusion is not evidence, and the breadth of one's other ideas is not the thing being tested. One premise meets one fact.

exercises.prompt: The premise was that a wish can correct a measurement. The measurement stands, and the beam is short. What does the inspection find?

choices.text: The premise stands, because the wish was sincere.
The premise does not stand. The wish did not change the measurement.
The premise stands, because a wish is metaphysically given and a measurement is not.
Every claim about measurement fails, including the claim that the beam has a length.

feedback.note: Checked against the fact, the premise fails: the wish did not lengthen the beam. Sincerity is not a correction of a measurement. The measurement reports an attribute that is given; the wish does not outrank it. The failure of this premise does not touch the claim that the beam has a length. Throwing that out would discard the fact the inspection used. One premise failed. The fact holds.

exercises.prompt: The inspection shows that the premise does not fit the fact. A teammate says to keep it, because the project needs the conclusion. What error is that?

choices.text: Shielding the premise because the conclusion was wanted.
A completed inspection, because a project is a form of proof.
Replacing the premise with one whose conclusion fits the fact.
Admitting that the fact holds and the conclusion gives way.

feedback.note: Needing the conclusion is not a reason for the premise. Keeping the premise on that ground shields it, which is the avoidance the inspection exists to stop. A project is not a proof. This teammate did not replace the premise or let the conclusion give. What the project needs is being treated as truth, which is pragmatism. A wanted destination does not rehabilitate the claim that failed against the fact.

exercises.prompt: Build the instruction that states what the inspection does.

feedback.note: Check the premise against the fact. Checking it against the wish shields it, because the wish made the conclusion attractive and does not make it true. Dropping every axiom discards ideas the clash never touched and calls that thoroughness. One premise is on trial. The fact is the standard. The rest of your knowledge is not collateral damage.

exercises.prompt: This premise failed the fact. A listener says no premise he holds is better off, including the axioms, so he will believe nothing derived. What is the mistake?

choices.text: He inspected one premise and kept the ideas that did not produce the clash.
He discarded every idea because one premise failed, which is more than the inspection showed.
He rewrote the fact in order to save the axioms.
He shielded the failed premise because the conclusion was useful.

feedback.note: The inspection showed that this premise does not fit the fact. It did not show that the axioms fail, or that every derived idea fails. Discarding them all is skepticism, treating one broken inference as the collapse of knowledge. He did not rewrite the fact, and he did not shield the failed premise. He overshot. The method keeps every claim that did not produce the clash, and it replaces a premise only where that premise failed.

exercises.prompt: The old premise has failed the fact. What must a replacement premise do?

choices.text: Sound more modest, whether or not the new conclusion fits the fact.
Be the emotional opposite of the old premise.
Make the new conclusion fit the fact.
Save as much of the old conclusion as the project still needs.

feedback.note: The replacement premise must make the new conclusion fit the fact, because that fit is what the old premise could not deliver. Modesty is a tone, not a test. The emotional opposite often misses the fact in the other direction. Saving the old conclusion because a project needs it shields the failed premise, which is pragmatism again. The standard for the new premise is the same fact that convicted the old one.

exercises.prompt: The premise that confidence guarantees the result failed, because the result failed. Which replacement fits the fact?

choices.text: A result must be checked against the facts, and confidence is not that check, so the failure stands.
Nothing about a result can be known, so the failure is neither real nor unreal.
The confidence was not intense enough, so the old premise stands in a stronger form.
The record of failure was a mood, so the result succeeded.

feedback.note: The fact is that the result failed. The replacement that fits says a result has to be checked against the facts, and confidence is not that check, so the failure stands. The claim that nothing about results can be known abandons the fact; that is skepticism. Intensifying the old premise shields it. Calling the record a mood rewrites the fact. Only the first replacement works, because it makes the new conclusion agree with what happened.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its job in the repair.

pairs.left: The faulty premise
pairs.right: The claim the fact refuted

pairs.left: The replacement premise
pairs.right: The claim that must yield a fitting conclusion

pairs.left: The new conclusion
pairs.right: What has to agree with the known fact

pairs.left: The known fact
pairs.right: The standard the new conclusion must meet

feedback.note: The faulty premise is the one the fact refuted. The replacement has one test: the conclusion it produces must fit that same fact. The new conclusion is not free to be any rebellion against the old one, and the fact is not revised to suit the replacement. The repair fails when a dramatic new premise is chosen and nobody checks the conclusion it yields, because the fact remains the standard.

exercises.prompt: Complete the test a replacement premise has to pass.

parts.text: It must make the new conclusion fit the

feedback.note: The new conclusion has to fit the fact. A mood, a slogan, or a project is the sort of thing that shielded the old premise, and using it as the test would repeat the failure. The replacement is not judged by how thoroughly it denounces the old view. It is judged by the conclusion it produces, because a conclusion that still misses the fact means the replacement is another bad premise.

exercises.prompt: The premise that agreement proves honesty failed, because he falsified the report. Someone replaces it with the claim that no one is ever honest. A second report checks out. Does the replacement pass?

choices.text: Yes, because it is the opposite of the old premise.
No. The new conclusion does not fit the fact that the second report checks out.
Yes, because a stronger suspicion is always the safer premise.
No, because the original premise should have been shielded.

feedback.note: The opposite of a bad premise is not automatically a repair. The claim that no one is ever honest yields a conclusion that the second report is a fraud, and that conclusion does not fit the fact that the report checks out. A safer-sounding suspicion is skepticism about character, not a premise fitted to the evidence. Shielding the original premise is the other error. The new conclusion has to fit the facts you actually have.

exercises.prompt: Facing a clash, a person repeats that one must check one's premises, then keeps the old premise and the old conclusion. What did the repetition accomplish?

choices.text: It performed the method, because saying the words is the method.
It named the method and did not use it. The premise was not traced, checked, or replaced.
It rewrote the fact, which is the step the method requires.
It supplied evidence, because words about a method are a kind of proof.

feedback.note: Repeating an injunction to check one's premises is not the check. The method is a sequence: the fact holds, the conclusion is traced to the premise that produced it, that premise is inspected, and a replacement must make the new conclusion fit the fact. He did none of those. The words are not evidence, and he did not rewrite the fact. He left the clash in place while sounding as if he were resolving it. The injunction names the method. It is not a substitute for the method.

exercises.prompt: Build the test the replacement has to meet.

feedback.note: The replacement premise must make the new conclusion fit the fact. Echoing the wish brings back the motive that shielded the old premise. Saving the old conclusion is what the method rules out once that conclusion has clashed with the fact. The test does not depend on the thinker's hopes, because a replacement that is only defiant, or only comforting, fails in the same way the original premise failed.

exercises.prompt: Each side of a voluntary exchange paid for what it received, and both gained. From the premise that every exchange exploits someone, you concluded that one side was sacrificed. Which repair fits the facts?

choices.text: Rewrite the gains as losses, so the exploitation premise survives.
Drop trade, rights, and identity together, because one conclusion failed.
Keep the exploitation premise, because the condemnation was the wanted conclusion.
Replace it: a voluntary trade of value for value is not exploitation, so this exchange stands as a trade.

feedback.note: The facts hold: both sides gained by a voluntary exchange. The conclusion that someone was sacrificed came from the premise that every exchange exploits, and that premise does not survive the facts. Shielding it because the condemnation was wanted protects a failed claim. Rewriting the gains rewrites the facts. Discarding trade, rights, and identity throws out ideas that did not produce this conclusion. The replacement fits the facts. That sequence is the method; the injunction only names it.
